final_dvs.pain_points: front desk gets pulled in ten directions, answering the phone gets delayed, estimates or walk-ins take priority, calls sit for a bit, interruptions when the shop gets slammed
final_dvs.pain_frame: Front desk gets pulled in ten directions when it’s busy, so answering the phone right away gets delayed while estimates or walk-ins take priority and calls sit for a bit.

transcript.caller: We have a girl at the front desk, she picks up fine. Not sure why I'd need this.
transcript.agent: Got it, if calls are already being answered, where do things get tight for you?

transcript.caller: Mostly when the shop gets slammed. People are helping customers, phones ring, we just call people back later.
transcript.agent: Makes sense, when those callbacks happen later, what tends to slip through?

transcript.caller: Honestly, never really counted misses. Feels like a solution looking for a problem to me.
transcript.agent: Fair enough, if it really is just occasional overflow, what made you take the call today?

transcript.caller: Had a minute between jobs and figured I’d hear you out, but I’m not looking to replace anybody.
transcript.agent: Got it, and I’m not talking about replacing anyone.When the shop gets slammed, is the bigger issue missed new work or interruptions for your team?

transcript.caller: Probably the interruptions more than anything. Front desk gets pulled in ten directions when it’s busy.
transcript.agent: Yeah, that sounds exhausting when everyone's getting pulled in different directions.When that happens, what usually gets delayed first?

transcript.caller: Usually answering the phone right away. Sometimes estimates or walk-ins take priority and calls sit for a bit.
transcript.agent: That makes sense, and it’s exhausting when the phone keeps losing out to everything else.

transcript.caller: Yeah, that's the business. Busy is good. We manage it fine and just return calls when we can.
transcript.agent: Right, and if calling people back is working well enough, what would have to start happening before it became worth fixing?

transcript.caller: If we were actually losing real jobs from it, maybe. But I’ve never really seen hard numbers on that.
transcript.agent: That’s fair, and you wouldn’t change anything on a guess.If even a couple callers gave up instead of waiting for the callback, would that matter to you?

transcript.caller: Sure, if people are actually dropping off and not booking, that’d matter. But I’d need to see that first.
transcript.agent: I hear you, seeing proof matters.Would it be worth a short look with Jay at where those delayed calls may be leaking jobs, just so you can judge it with real data?

transcript.caller: Alright, as a backup layer I can see it. Book your demo. +16174000005
transcript.agent: Got it, as a backup layer makes sense. Sounds good, and before I move that forward, what kind of shop are you in?

transcript.caller: Auto body shop, collision repair mainly. We're in Boston.
transcript.agent: Got it, collision repair in Boston.

transcript.caller: Yep, that’s right. What exactly does this thing do when we can’t get to the phone?
transcript.agent: When your team’s tied up, it answers right away, handles the caller like a front desk backup, and helps keep new jobs from slipping while your staff stays focused.Want me to give you the quick version of how it works for a collision shop?

transcript.caller: Yeah, quick version’s fine. Keep it short.
transcript.agent: Sure, when your front desk is tied up, it picks up right away, handles basic intake, and makes sure callers don’t drift to the next shop.Want the version of what that sounds like for your customers?

transcript.caller: Yeah, go ahead. What's it actually sound like to someone calling in?
transcript.agent: Got it, to your caller it sounds like a calm front desk backup that answers right away, gets the key details, and helps move the job forward instead of sending them to voicemail.Want the caller experience version or the shop workflow version?

transcript.caller: Shop workflow version. I care more about how it helps us without creating extra work.
transcript.agent: It takes the first ring off your team, grabs the key info up front, and keeps your front desk from bouncing between walk-ins, estimates, and a ringing line.Would it help to see what that missed-call leak could look like in your shop with rough numbers?

transcript.caller: Maybe, but I’m not convinced we’re leaking enough to matter. Give me the rough version.
transcript.agent: Fair enough, mind if I do a quick back-of-the-napkin version with your numbers?

transcript.caller: Alright, quick version. But keep it simple.
transcript.agent: Got it, about how many calls a day hit voicemail when the shop gets slammed, 2, 5, or 10?

transcript.caller: Closer to 2 or 3 on a busy day, not 10.
transcript.agent: Got it, let’s call it 3 on a busy day.Of those, what share do you think would actually turn into work if you answered right away, maybe 25% or 50%?

transcript.caller: Maybe half, if they’re calling around and we get them first.
transcript.agent: Got it, and what’s your average repair ticket, roughly?

transcript.caller: Roughly eleven hundred bucks on average, give or take.
transcript.agent: Alright, using that rough version, if 3 calls a day slip to voicemail and half would have booked at about $1,100, that adds up fast. So on your rough numbers, that’s about $8,250 a week that could slip when calls sit instead of getting answered.Does that feel in the ballpark?

transcript.caller: Maybe on paper, sure. Still sounds high, but I get the point if it’s just a backup.
transcript.agent: Totally fair, and even if we cut that down hard, it still points to money slipping when your front desk is tied up.

transcript.caller: Yeah, if it’s truly just covering overflow and not replacing anybody, I can at least take a look.
transcript.agent: Perfect, that’s all I was hoping for.Let me grab a few details to get you booked.

transcript.caller: Alright, go ahead. What do you need from me?
transcript.agent: Perfect, and since you already gave me your number, what’s the best name to put on the booking?

transcript.caller: Dave Kowalski.
transcript.agent: Got it, Dave.And your company name?

transcript.caller: Kowalski Auto Body.
transcript.agent: Thanks, and is the number you're calling from the best contact number to reach you?

transcript.caller: Yeah, this number’s fine.
transcript.agent: Perfect, I’ve got that as your best number.

transcript.caller: Alright. When’s this demo supposed to happen?
transcript.agent: We’re just finishing your details first, and then I’ll get to the time.

transcript.caller: Alright, just don’t make this a whole big thing.
transcript.agent: Absolutely, I’ll keep it simple. Of course, Dave.Would you prefer later today or tomorrow for the demo?

transcript.caller: Tomorrow’s better. Late morning if you’ve got it.

transcript.caller: 2:30 works. Put me down for that.
transcript.agent: So that’s tomorrow at 2:30 pm Eastern, correct?

transcript.caller: Yeah, tomorrow at 2:30 Eastern works.
transcript.agent: Perfect.One sec — finishing that up.  Perfect, Dave, you’re booked for tomorrow at 2:30 Eastern, and a confirmation is coming your way.Is there anything else I can help you with?

transcript.caller: No, that’s it. I’ll keep an eye out for the confirmation.
transcript.agent: Glad we got it set, Dave, and you’ll get a confirmation with the details shortly.
